options.a: Place the probe under the front of the tongue and remove it after 30 seconds
options.b: Place the probe sublingually 5 minutes after the patient finishes a hot drink
options.c: Place the probe in the posterior sublingual pocket and wait for the signal
options.d: Hold the probe between the cheek and gum and wait for the signal

distractorExplanations.a: Anterior placement under the tongue reads low, and an electronic probe stays in until the device signals, not for a fixed 30 seconds.
distractorExplanations.b: After hot or cold drinks the wait is about 15-30 minutes; 5 minutes leaves the oral reading falsely elevated.
distractorExplanations.d: Buccal (cheek) placement is away from the sublingual heat pocket near the lingual artery and gives a falsely low reading.

options.a: Rise in blood pressure with a slowed pulse on standing
options.b: Pulse increase of 5 beats/min with stable blood pressure
options.c: Mild rise in respiratory rate with no change in blood pressure
options.d: Significant drop in blood pressure with dizziness on standing

distractorExplanations.a: Orthostatic hypotension is a fall in BP with a compensatory pulse rise; a BP rise with bradycardia is the opposite pattern.
distractorExplanations.b: A small pulse rise with steady BP is a normal postural response; orthostatic criteria are a drop of 20 systolic or 10 diastolic.
distractorExplanations.c: Tachypnea without any BP drop is nonspecific and does not meet the definition of orthostatic hypotension.

options.a: Apply the tourniquet and select the vein before checking the order
options.b: Identify the patient by room number and date of birth, then label tubes
options.c: Assemble equipment and label the tubes before the patient is seated
options.d: Identify the patient using two identifiers and verify the order

distractorExplanations.a: Wrong sequence: tourniquet and vein selection come after patient identification and order verification, not before.
distractorExplanations.b: A room number is not an acceptable identifier, and tubes are labeled after collection in the patient's presence.
distractorExplanations.c: Pre-labeling tubes before the draw is a classic mislabeling risk; labels go on after collection at the chairside.

options.a: Use non-latex gloves per facility protocol
options.b: Use powder-free latex gloves to limit exposure
options.c: Use latex gloves if the allergy is only a mild rash
options.d: Skip gloves and perform hand hygiene before and after

distractorExplanations.b: Powder-free latex still carries latex proteins that trigger reactions; an allergic patient needs non-latex products.
distractorExplanations.c: A mild past reaction does not make latex safe; reactions can escalate, so any reported latex allergy calls for non-latex gloves.
distractorExplanations.d: Hand hygiene does not replace gloves when contact with blood or body fluids is anticipated under Standard Precautions.

options.a: Puncture the center pad of the fingertip, where nerve endings are fewest
options.b: Wipe away the first drop and use a subsequent drop per device instructions
options.c: Squeeze firmly from the base toward the tip to form a large hanging drop
options.d: Clean the site with alcohol and puncture right away, before the alcohol dries

distractorExplanations.a: The center pad is the most sensitive area; the puncture goes on the side of the fingertip pad of the middle or ring finger.
distractorExplanations.c: Firm squeezing (milking) dilutes the drop with tissue fluid and can hemolyze it; only gentle pressure is used.
distractorExplanations.d: Wet alcohol on the site can hemolyze and dilute the sample and stings; the site must air-dry before the puncture.

options.a: Remove the needle, apply pressure, lower the head, and call for help
options.b: Remove the needle and have the patient stand to improve circulation
options.c: Finish filling the current tube quickly, then remove the needle
options.d: Remove the needle and leave the patient seated alone while you get water

distractorExplanations.b: Standing a near-syncopal patient raises the fall risk; the patient stays seated or lying with the head lowered.
distractorExplanations.c: Continuing the draw risks needle injury if the patient loses consciousness; the draw is stopped at the first sign.
distractorExplanations.d: A patient at risk of syncope must not be left unattended; stay with the patient and call for help instead.

options.a: Use body-temperature solution and aim directly at the eardrum
options.b: Use body-temperature solution and aim along the canal wall
options.c: Use cool tap water and aim along the upper canal wall
options.d: Pull the adult auricle down and back, then irrigate at high pressure

distractorExplanations.a: Aiming the stream at the tympanic membrane risks perforation; the flow is directed along the superior canal wall.
distractorExplanations.c: Solution that is not near body temperature stimulates the vestibular system and causes vertigo and nausea.
distractorExplanations.d: Down and back is the pediatric pinna pull; adults need up and back, and high pressure risks canal or eardrum injury.

aama-cma-readiness-check-clinical-010.explanation: Warm (body-temperature) irrigation aimed along the canal reduces dizziness/injury risk; contraindications must be screened. Irrigate per provider order/protocol.

options.a: Gloves first, then gown, mask/respirator, and eye protection last
options.b: Mask/respirator, eye protection, gloves, then gown tied over the gloves
options.c: Gown, mask/respirator as indicated, eye protection if needed, then gloves
options.d: Gown, gloves, mask/respirator, then eye protection adjusted with gloved hands

distractorExplanations.a: Gloves are donned last so they cover the gown cuffs; putting them on first reverses the CDC donning order.
distractorExplanations.b: The gown goes on before gloves; glove cuffs must extend over the gown cuffs, not sit under the gown.
distractorExplanations.d: Gloves come after mask and eye protection; donning them second means touching face PPE with gloved hands.

options.a: The pooled exudate on the old dressing after it is removed
options.b: The wound edges and surrounding skin before any cleansing
options.c: The deepest cleanest portion of the wound after removing surface debris
options.d: The surface pus and slough before rinsing, where bacteria are densest

distractorExplanations.a: Dressing exudate is contaminated with surface colonizers and does not reflect the current wound-bed flora.
distractorExplanations.b: Uncleansed edges and skin add skin flora to the culture; the cleansed wound bed is sampled instead.
distractorExplanations.d: Surface pus and slough hold colonizing bacteria, not the infecting organism; debris is removed before swabbing.

aama-cma-readiness-check-clinical-013.explanation: Culture accuracy improves when surface contaminants are cleared and the active wound bed is sampled per protocol. Follow the facility collection protocol.

options.a: Explaining the cytology result to the patient when the report arrives
options.b: Deciding whether the patient needs an HPV co-test based on age
options.c: Labeling specimens correctly and preparing the patient per protocol
options.d: Labeling the vial after it leaves the room, together with the requisition

distractorExplanations.a: Interpreting and explaining cytology results is a provider responsibility, not part of the MA's assisting role.
distractorExplanations.b: Choosing HPV co-testing is a provider order based on screening guidelines, not an MA decision.
distractorExplanations.d: Specimens are labeled in the patient's presence right after collection; labeling later away from the patient risks mix-ups.

options.a: Swallowed whole with water for steady absorption
options.b: Sublingually for rapid absorption when ordered
options.c: Intramuscularly into the deltoid for rapid relief
options.d: Transdermally as a patch for rapid relief of pain

distractorExplanations.a: Swallowed nitroglycerin undergoes heavy first-pass liver metabolism; acute angina doses are given sublingually.
distractorExplanations.c: Nitroglycerin is not given IM for angina; the acute routes are sublingual tablet or spray (IV in hospital).
distractorExplanations.d: Nitroglycerin patches give slow, long-acting prophylaxis; they do not relieve an acute angina attack.

options.a: Pancreatic beta cells
options.b: Pancreatic alpha cells
options.c: Adrenal medulla
options.d: Posterior pituitary

distractorExplanations.b: Alpha cells of the islets of Langerhans secrete glucagon, which raises blood glucose; insulin comes from beta cells.
distractorExplanations.c: Adrenal medulla produces catecholamines.
distractorExplanations.d: Posterior pituitary releases ADH and oxytocin.

options.a: Closer to the trunk or point of origin
options.b: Farther from the trunk or point of origin
options.c: Closer to the front surface of the body
options.d: Closer to the midline of the body

distractorExplanations.c: Closer to the front of the body is anterior (ventral); proximal refers to nearness to the trunk or origin.
distractorExplanations.d: Closer to the midline is medial; proximal describes position along a limb relative to its attachment.
distractorExplanations.b: That defines distal.

options.a: Inhaled corticosteroid controller
options.b: Anticholinergic bronchodilator
options.c: Leukotriene receptor antagonist
options.d: Beta-2 agonist bronchodilator

distractorExplanations.a: Inhaled corticosteroids such as fluticasone reduce airway inflammation; albuterol is a short-acting beta-2 agonist.
distractorExplanations.b: Anticholinergic bronchodilators are ipratropium and tiotropium; albuterol acts on beta-2 adrenergic receptors.
distractorExplanations.c: Leukotriene receptor antagonists are oral controllers such as montelukast, not a rescue bronchodilator like albuterol.

options.a: Hyponatremia
options.b: Hypokalemia
options.c: Hypocalcemia
options.d: Hyperkalemia

distractorExplanations.a: Sodium disorders have different presentations.
distractorExplanations.b: Hypokalemia more often causes U waves/flattened T waves.
distractorExplanations.c: Hypocalcemia affects QT interval differently.

options.a: Produce bile for fat digestion
options.b: Store and concentrate bile
options.c: Secrete digestive enzymes
options.d: Filter blood urea

distractorExplanations.a: The liver produces bile; the gallbladder only stores and concentrates it and releases it after fatty meals.
distractorExplanations.c: Digestive enzymes such as lipase, amylase and trypsin come from the pancreas, not the gallbladder.
distractorExplanations.d: Kidneys filter urea.

options.a: Subcutaneously into the abdomen
options.b: Intravenously by the patient at home
options.c: Subcutaneously into the back of the upper arm
options.d: Intramuscularly into the mid-outer thigh

distractorExplanations.c: Subcutaneous absorption is slower; epinephrine auto-injectors are labeled for IM use in the anterolateral thigh.
distractorExplanations.a: IM thigh is preferred over SQ abdomen for auto-injectors.
distractorExplanations.b: Patients do not self-administer IV epinephrine at home.

options.a: Procedures and services performed
options.b: Supplies, drugs, and equipment
options.c: Physician work and practice expense values
options.d: Diagnoses and reasons for encounter

distractorExplanations.a: Procedures and services are reported with CPT (HCPCS Level I), while ICD-10-CM reports diagnoses.
distractorExplanations.b: Supplies, drugs and DME are reported with HCPCS Level II codes, not ICD-10-CM diagnosis codes.
distractorExplanations.c: Work and practice expense values are RVUs in the Medicare physician fee schedule, not ICD-10-CM codes.

options.a: Diagnoses and reasons for the visit
options.b: Durable medical equipment and supplies
options.c: Inpatient hospital procedures
options.d: Procedures and services performed

distractorExplanations.a: Diagnoses and visit reasons are reported with ICD-10-CM; CPT reports what the provider did.
distractorExplanations.b: DME and supplies are reported with HCPCS Level II codes, not CPT (HCPCS Level I).
distractorExplanations.c: Inpatient hospital procedures are coded with ICD-10-PCS; CPT covers outpatient and physician services.

options.a: Instruct overnight fasting per protocol and confirm instructions
options.b: Instruct a 4-hour fast with only clear juice allowed beforehand
options.c: Schedule a late-afternoon draw so the patient can eat breakfast
options.d: Instruct fasting and tell the patient to avoid drinking water too

distractorExplanations.b: A fasting lipid panel usually needs a 9-12 hour fast with water only; juice contains sugar and 4 hours is too short.
distractorExplanations.c: Eating breakfast breaks the fast and raises triglycerides, so the sample would no longer be a fasting specimen.
distractorExplanations.d: Water is permitted and encouraged during a lab fast; withholding it causes dehydration and a harder draw.

options.a: Bill the patient for the full charge before reviewing the denial reason
options.b: Resubmit the same claim unchanged to see if it processes
options.c: Review documentation and payer policy, then follow appeal/correction procedures
options.d: Add a diagnosis code from the patient's problem list that meets payer criteria

distractorExplanations.a: Billing the patient before reviewing the denial skips the appeal and may breach the payer contract if no ABN or waiver exists.
distractorExplanations.b: An unchanged resubmission is treated as a duplicate and denied again; the cause of the denial must be addressed first.
distractorExplanations.d: Codes must reflect conditions documented for that encounter; adding a problem-list diagnosis to meet criteria is upcoding.

options.a: A copy of the patient's insurance card kept on file
options.b: Valid patient authorization meeting HIPAA requirements
options.c: The patient's verbal OK given by phone to the front-desk staff
options.d: A signed Notice of Privacy Practices acknowledgment

distractorExplanations.a: An insurance card supports billing; it does not authorize disclosure of PHI to an unrelated third party.
distractorExplanations.c: A HIPAA authorization must be written and signed with required elements; a verbal OK by phone does not qualify.
distractorExplanations.d: The NPP acknowledgment only confirms the patient received the notice; it is not an authorization to release PHI.

options.a: Notify a beneficiary that Medicaid will pay as the secondary payer
options.b: Serve as the patient's consent to the procedure being performed
options.c: Notify an inpatient of the right to appeal a hospital discharge
options.d: Notify a beneficiary that Medicare may not pay for a service

distractorExplanations.a: Secondary-payer order is handled by coordination of benefits, not by the Advance Beneficiary Notice.
distractorExplanations.b: The ABN is a financial liability notice; informed consent for the procedure is a separate clinical document.
distractorExplanations.c: Discharge appeal rights are given on the Important Message from Medicare (IM), not on the outpatient ABN.

options.a: Prior visit diagnoses and the patient's medication history
options.b: The allowed amount the payer will reimburse for each CPT code
options.c: Coverage active dates, plan type, and referral/authorization needs
options.d: That the patient's coverage was active on their last visit date

distractorExplanations.a: Diagnoses and medication history are clinical intake data; eligibility checks confirm coverage and benefit rules.
distractorExplanations.b: Allowed amounts come from the payer contract and claim adjudication, not from a front-end eligibility check.
distractorExplanations.d: Eligibility must be verified for the current date of service; coverage at a previous visit may have lapsed.

options.a: Explain to the patient what the payer paid and what they owe
options.b: Capture diagnoses and services for billing from the visit
options.c: Serve as the claim form transmitted to the payer for the visit
options.d: Record the patient's history and exam findings for the visit

distractorExplanations.a: Payer payment and patient balance are explained on the EOB or patient statement, not on the superbill.
distractorExplanations.c: The claim sent to the payer is the CMS-1500 or 837P built from the superbill, not the superbill itself.
distractorExplanations.d: History and exam findings are recorded in the progress note; the superbill only captures codes for billing.

options.a: Follow written protocols and escalate urgent symptoms to a licensed clinician
options.b: Advise home care for chest pain when the caller says it feels like simple heartburn
options.c: Call in a refill of the caller's antibiotic if symptoms have recurred
options.d: Book the next routine opening for any caller who reports severe symptoms

distractorExplanations.b: Chest pain is escalated per protocol even if described as heartburn; the MA cannot downgrade possible cardiac symptoms.
distractorExplanations.c: Authorizing an antibiotic refill is prescribing, which is outside MA scope without a provider order.
distractorExplanations.d: Severe symptoms require immediate escalation or emergency direction under the protocol, not a routine appointment.

options.a: Track unpaid claims/balances by how long they have been outstanding
options.b: Compare each payer's allowed amounts against the fee schedule
options.c: Record daily charges, payments, and adjustments posted
options.d: List claims rejected by the clearinghouse before payer submission

distractorExplanations.b: Comparing allowed amounts to the fee schedule is payer contract analysis, not an aging of outstanding balances.
distractorExplanations.c: Daily charges, payments and adjustments are recorded on the day sheet (daily journal), not the AR aging report.
distractorExplanations.d: Clearinghouse rejections appear on the rejection/edit report; aging buckets balances by days outstanding.

options.a: Draw a line through the error and write the correction above it, unsigned
options.b: Black out the error fully, initial and date it, then write the correction
options.c: Rewrite the whole page correctly and discard the original page
options.d: Draw a single line through the error, initial, date, and write the correction

distractorExplanations.a: A correction must be initialed and dated so the author and timing are traceable; an unsigned change is not acceptable.
distractorExplanations.b: Blacking out obliterates the original entry; it must stay legible under a single line to avoid suspicion of tampering.
distractorExplanations.c: Discarding the original page destroys part of the legal record, which is treated as tampering.

options.a: A payer requires approval before covering certain services or medications
options.b: A patient is seen by an out-of-network provider for a covered emergency
options.c: A patient on a PPO plan books a visit with an in-network specialist
options.d: A patient requests copies of their records from the practice

distractorExplanations.b: Federal rules bar plans from requiring prior authorization for emergency services, including out-of-network ER care.
distractorExplanations.c: PPO plans generally allow in-network specialist visits without a referral or prior authorization; that is an HMO rule.
distractorExplanations.d: A records request falls under the HIPAA right of access, which involves no payer approval at all.

options.a: PPO plans generally require a PCP referral before any specialist visit
options.b: A referral approved once covers unlimited specialist visits for the year
options.c: Many HMO plans require referrals/authorizations before specialty care
options.d: Original Medicare Part B requires a PCP referral for every specialist visit

distractorExplanations.a: PPOs typically allow self-referral to specialists; the PCP-referral gatekeeper model is characteristic of HMOs.
distractorExplanations.b: Referrals usually specify a visit count and expiration date; they do not authorize unlimited visits for a year.
distractorExplanations.d: Original Medicare does not require PCP referrals for specialists; referral rules apply in many Medicare Advantage HMOs.

options.a: De-identified health data stripped of the 18 identifiers
options.b: Employment records held by a covered entity as employer
options.c: Education records covered by FERPA
options.d: Protected health information (PHI)

distractorExplanations.a: Data de-identified under the Safe Harbor method (18 identifiers removed) is no longer PHI under the Privacy Rule.
distractorExplanations.b: Employment records a covered entity holds in its role as employer are excluded from the HIPAA definition of PHI.
distractorExplanations.c: Education records covered by FERPA are expressly excluded from PHI; FERPA, not HIPAA, governs them.

options.a: Sign the form after the MA explains the surgical risks
options.b: Be told risks, benefits, and alternatives and agree voluntarily
options.c: Be told the risks and benefits, without discussing alternatives
options.d: Be told risks and benefits after the procedure has been completed

distractorExplanations.a: Disclosing procedure risks is the provider's duty; the MA may witness the signature but cannot obtain informed consent.
distractorExplanations.c: Alternatives, including no treatment, are a required element of informed consent, not an optional extra.
distractorExplanations.d: Consent must be obtained before the procedure; disclosure afterward cannot make the treatment consented.

aama-cma-readiness-check-law-ethics-002.explanation: Informed consent is voluntary agreement after adequate disclosure and opportunity for questions. Information must be given in understandable terms.

options.a: A toddler with scattered bruises over the shins and knees from active play
options.b: A child with unexplained patterned bruises and inconsistent history
options.c: A child whose parent declines a flu vaccine after counseling
options.d: A child who misses one appointment with no other concerns noted

distractorExplanations.a: Bruises over bony prominences like shins and knees in active toddlers are typical accidental injuries, not a red flag.
distractorExplanations.c: Declining one vaccine after counseling is a parental decision and not, by itself, reasonable suspicion of neglect.
distractorExplanations.d: A single missed appointment without other concerns does not meet the reasonable-suspicion threshold for reporting.

options.a: Provide hepatitis B vaccine at the employee's own cost
options.b: Review the exposure control plan every three years
options.c: Provide training, PPE, and an exposure control plan
options.d: Provide training at hire, with refresher training every 3 years

distractorExplanations.a: The hepatitis B vaccine series must be offered at no cost to at-risk employees within 10 working days of assignment.
distractorExplanations.b: The exposure control plan must be reviewed and updated at least annually, not every three years.
distractorExplanations.d: Bloodborne pathogens training is required at initial assignment and at least annually, not every 3 years.

options.a: Schedule appointments and verify patients' insurance eligibility
options.b: Perform CLIA-waived tests if trained and authorized
options.c: Take vital signs under supervision/protocol
options.d: Independently diagnose disease and prescribe medication

distractorExplanations.a: Scheduling and eligibility checks are routine administrative MA duties, so they are not something an MA is barred from.
distractorExplanations.b: CLIA-waived testing is often within trained MA scope.
distractorExplanations.c: Vitals are common MA duties.

options.a: Failure to meet the standard of care with no resulting harm
options.b: Failure to meet the standard of care causing harm
options.c: Intentional touching of a patient without consent
options.d: An unexpected poor outcome despite proper care

distractorExplanations.a: Negligence requires all four Ds; a breach without damages (harm) does not support a malpractice claim.
distractorExplanations.c: Intentional unconsented touching is battery, an intentional tort, rather than negligence.
distractorExplanations.d: A poor outcome when the standard of care was met is not negligence; there is no breach of duty.

options.a: Names a healthcare proxy to make medical decisions
options.b: States wishes about life-sustaining treatment
options.c: Is a physician order to withhold CPR in any setting
options.d: Directs how the patient's property is distributed

distractorExplanations.a: Naming a proxy is done in a durable power of attorney for health care, a separate advance directive.
distractorExplanations.c: A DNR or POLST is a medical order signed by a clinician; a living will is the patient's own statement of wishes.
distractorExplanations.d: Distribution of property is handled by a last will and testament, not by a living will.

aama-cma-readiness-check-law-ethics-007.explanation: Living wills document preferences for end-of-life/life-sustaining care when the patient lacks capacity. It applies when the patient cannot communicate.

options.a: Verifying identity before releasing results
options.b: Leaving a minimal appointment reminder on voicemail
options.c: Discussing a case with the care team for treatment
options.d: Posting a patient's diagnosis on social media

distractorExplanations.b: HIPAA permits limited appointment reminders by voicemail using minimum necessary information unless the patient objects.
distractorExplanations.a: Identity verification protects against wrongful disclosure.
distractorExplanations.c: Treatment-related sharing with the care team is permitted.

options.a: Moderately complex and requires proficiency testing
options.b: Exempt from needing any CLIA certificate when done in a physician office
options.c: Simple with low risk of erroneous results when directions are followed
options.d: Limited to licensed lab scientists under a lab director's review

distractorExplanations.a: Proficiency testing applies to moderate- and high-complexity testing; waived tests are not moderate complexity.
distractorExplanations.b: Offices performing waived tests still need a CLIA Certificate of Waiver and must follow manufacturer instructions.
distractorExplanations.d: Licensed-scientist personnel rules describe high-complexity testing; trained MAs may perform waived tests.

options.a: Threatening a patient with an injection so they comply
options.b: Performing a procedure after valid informed consent
options.c: Touching or treating a patient without consent
options.d: Sharing a patient's diagnosis with a coworker not involved in care

distractorExplanations.a: A threat causing fear of imminent contact is assault; battery requires actual unconsented touching.
distractorExplanations.d: Sharing a diagnosis with an uninvolved coworker is a privacy breach (invasion of privacy), not battery.
distractorExplanations.b: Consented care is not battery.

options.a: Only patients with a known infection diagnosis pose risk
options.b: Hand hygiene can be skipped if gloves were worn throughout
options.c: Blood and certain body fluids of all patients may be infectious
options.d: Sweat and intact skin are handled as potentially infectious material

distractorExplanations.a: Standard Precautions exist because undiagnosed, asymptomatic patients can transmit bloodborne infections.
distractorExplanations.b: Gloves can have defects and hands become contaminated during removal, so hand hygiene is required after gloves.
distractorExplanations.d: Standard Precautions cover blood, body fluids, secretions and excretions except sweat; intact skin is not OPIM.

options.a: Emergency aid given by an on-duty clinician during a scheduled clinic shift
options.b: Grossly negligent emergency aid given at a roadside accident scene
options.c: Emergency aid given for a fee charged to the patient afterward
options.d: Reasonable emergency aid given in good faith outside a duty-to-treat setting

distractorExplanations.a: Good Samaritan laws protect volunteers without a pre-existing duty; on-duty care is judged by the normal standard of care.
distractorExplanations.b: Gross negligence and willful misconduct are excluded from Good Samaritan protection in virtually every state.
distractorExplanations.c: Charging a fee for the aid generally removes Good Samaritan protection, which covers uncompensated help.

aama-cma-readiness-check-law-ethics-012.explanation: Good Samaritan laws generally shield good-faith emergency helpers acting reasonably; they do not cover intentional misconduct or fraud. Specific protections vary by state.

options.a: Minors may consent to any care once they turn 16 in every state
options.b: A grandparent or school nurse may consent if a parent is not reachable
options.c: Emancipated minors still need a parent's signature for routine care
options.d: Parents/guardians usually consent for minors, with specific exceptions

distractorExplanations.a: There is no uniform age-16 rule; the age of majority and minor-consent exceptions vary by state and service.
distractorExplanations.b: Grandparents and school nurses are not default decision-makers without legal guardianship or written authorization.
distractorExplanations.c: Emancipated minors consent to their own care; requiring a parent's signature confuses them with unemancipated minors.

aama-cma-readiness-check-law-ethics-013.explanation: Parental/guardian consent is usual, but state laws create exceptions for emancipated minors and certain sensitive services. Examples of exceptions include certain reproductive and mental health services, which vary by state.

options.a: Placed in the patient's medical record with the visit note
options.b: Written days later once everyone's account has been gathered
options.c: Written to include opinions about who was at fault
options.d: Filed objectively, promptly, and per facility policy

distractorExplanations.a: Incident reports are risk-management documents kept out of the chart; the chart records only the clinical facts.
distractorExplanations.b: Incident reports are completed promptly, usually the same shift, while details are accurate, not days later.
distractorExplanations.c: Incident reports state objective facts only; opinions or blame about fault are excluded.

aama-cma-readiness-check-law-ethics-014.explanation: Incident reports document facts for risk management; they are handled per policy and are not public notices. Avoid blaming language.

options.a: Overriding a capacitated patient's refusal to prevent possible harm
options.b: Distributing limited clinic resources fairly among all patients
options.c: Respecting a capacitated patient's informed decisions about care
options.d: Avoiding actions that may harm the patient during care

distractorExplanations.a: Overriding a capacitated refusal is paternalism, putting beneficence above autonomy rather than respecting it.
distractorExplanations.b: Fair distribution of limited resources describes the principle of justice, not autonomy.
distractorExplanations.d: Avoiding harm is the principle of nonmaleficence; autonomy concerns the patient's right to decide.
